details:
**Dipped in the River Styx by Thetis (the heel)**
Achilles's mother, the sea nymph Thetis, dipped him as a baby in the River Styx to make him invulnerable, but the heel she held him by stayed dry and remained his one weak spot. In another version she put him in a fire, sometimes after anointing him with ambrosia, to burn away his mortal parts, but Peleus interrupted her. The phrase "Achilles' heel" comes from this story.

**Killed by Paris's arrow**
Achilles was killed when the Trojan prince Paris shot him in the heel (or ankle) with an arrow, which Apollo guided and which some accounts say was poisoned. In some versions this happened at the temple of Thymbraean Apollo, where Achilles had gone to meet the Trojan princess Polyxena, with whom he had fallen in love.

**Patroclus**
Achilles's closest friend (in some later readings, his lover). While Achilles refused to fight, Patroclus went into battle wearing Achilles's armor to rally the Greeks and was killed by Hector with help from Apollo. His death brought Achilles back into the war. After Achilles died, their ashes were mixed in a single urn.

**Killing Hector and dragging his body around Troy**
To avenge Patroclus, Achilles killed the Trojan champion Hector, after Athena tricked Hector into standing and fighting by appearing as his brother Deiphobus. Achilles then dragged Hector's corpse behind his chariot around the walls of Troy (three times in many accounts) and around Patroclus's tomb. In Book 24 of the Iliad, Priam, Hecuba's husband, sneaked into the Greek camp, kissed Achilles's hands, and ransomed the body for burial.

**Briseis and the quarrel with Agamemnon**
At the start of the Iliad, Agamemnon was forced to give back his captive Chryseis, daughter of a priest of Apollo, and took Achilles's captive concubine Briseis to replace her. Achilles withdrew from the fighting in anger. Even an embassy led by his old tutor Phoenix, who told him the cautionary story of Meleager and offered many gifts, could not bring him back.

**"Sing, goddess, the rage of Achilles"**
The opening line of Homer's Iliad, which names its subject as the wrath (menis) of Achilles, "son of Peleus." The poem covers a few weeks near the end of the Trojan War, from his quarrel with Agamemnon to Hector's funeral.

**Penthesilea and Thersites**
Achilles killed Penthesilea, the Amazon queen who fought for Troy, and fell in love with her as she died, or as he took off her helmet. When the ugly, foul-mouthed soldier Thersites mocked his grief (in some versions gouging out the dead queen's eyes), Achilles killed him with a blow.

**Shield of Achilles**
After Patroclus lost Achilles's armor to Hector, Thetis asked Hephaestus to forge new armor. Book 18 of the Iliad describes the shield in detail: the earth, sky, sea, sun, moon, and constellations (Pleiades, Hyades, Orion, and the Bear); a city at peace with a wedding and a lawsuit, and a city at war; plowing, harvesting, a vineyard, herds, and a dance, all surrounded by the stream of Ocean.

**Disguised as a girl at the court of Lycomedes on Skyros**
Knowing Achilles would die if he went to Troy, Thetis hid him dressed as a girl (sometimes called Pyrrha or Aissa) among the daughters of King Lycomedes on Skyros. Odysseus exposed him by offering gifts of jewelry with weapons hidden among them, sometimes adding a trumpet alarm, and Achilles grabbed the weapons.

**Deidamia and Neoptolemus**
While hiding on Skyros, Achilles fathered Neoptolemus (also called Pyrrhus) with Lycomedes's daughter Deidamia. The seer Helenus prophesied that the Greeks needed Neoptolemus to take Troy, and after Achilles died, his ghost demanded that Polyxena be sacrificed on his tomb.

**Contest between Ajax and Odysseus for his armor**
After Achilles died, Telamonian Ajax (Ajax the Greater) and Odysseus each claimed his divine armor. When it was awarded to Odysseus, Ajax went mad and killed himself.

**Fighting the river god Scamander**
In Book 21 of the Iliad, Achilles killed so many Trojans that their bodies choked the river Scamander (Xanthus). The angry river god rose up to drown him, and Hephaestus saved Achilles by driving back the river with fire.

**Memnon**
After the events of the Iliad, Achilles killed Memnon, the Ethiopian king and son of Eos (Dawn) and Tithonus, who had killed Nestor's son Antilochus while Antilochus was saving his father. Memnon's mourning followers were turned into birds (the Memnonides).

**Marriage of Peleus and Thetis and the prophecy**
Zeus and Poseidon both wanted Thetis until a prophecy (from Themis or Prometheus) warned that her son would be greater than his father. She was married instead to the mortal Peleus, who had to wrestle her while she changed shapes. At their wedding, Eris threw in the golden apple that led to the Judgment of Paris. Chiron gave Peleus an ash spear and Poseidon gave the immortal horses Balius and Xanthus, which Achilles later used at Troy.

**Telephus healed by his spear**
On the way to Troy, Achilles wounded Telephus, king of Mysia, with his spear. An oracle said only the weapon that caused the wound could heal it, so Telephus, in one version by threatening the infant Orestes, made the Greeks help him, and Achilles cured him with rust scraped from the spear. Achilles was raised and taught by the centaur Chiron, who made him a great runner, and his speed is the basis of Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise.
